eventops.title: EventOps
eventops.summary: Calendar, staff and finances for your events company.
eventops.metaTitle: EventOps: management system for event companies
eventops.metaDescription: EventOps brings the calendar, clients, staff and finances of an event company into a single system. A ShippersLab own product, in production.

features.title: Calendar
features.body: All events for the month, week or day in a single view, with the site visit, setup, sound check and teardown of each one.

features.title: Quotes
features.body: Pick services from your list and the total adds up on its own. The quote is exported as a PDF with your logo, ready to send to the client.

features.title: Staff
features.body: Add team members to each date with their role and see who is free before assigning them, so no event is left short-handed.

features.title: Finances
features.body: Deposits and installments in pesos or dollars, per-event and general expenses, and a monthly summary of income and expenses. All the data can be exported to CSV.

features.title: Clients
features.body: Each client with contact details, source, history and next event. Individuals, companies and venues in a single record.

features.title: Team
features.body: Everyone at the company signs in with their own user. Invitations are sent by email and each company only sees its own data.

eventops.lead: The calendar, clients, staff and finances of your event company in a single system. A ShippersLab own product, in production.
eventops.overview: An event company handles dates, teams, clients and payments all at once. When that information is scattered across spreadsheets and messages, it is easy for two events to overlap, for staff to be missing, or for nobody to know exactly how much money came in and how much is still owed.
eventops.approach: EventOps brings the whole operation into a single system. Each event has its client, its team and its money movements, and the calendar shows at a glance what needs to happen and when. We designed it around how an event company works, so everyone always sees the same information.
eventops.flowDescription: Each event is entered once and everything else comes from it. Nothing has to be copied into another spreadsheet.

flow.title: Create the event
flow.body: The event is created with its client and related dates are added: site visit, setup, sound check and teardown. They all show up in the calendar and the system warns when two dates overlap.

flow.title: Build the quote
flow.body: Services such as sound, lighting or an LED screen are picked from the list and the total is calculated automatically. The quote downloads as a PDF with the company logo.

flow.title: Assign the staff
flow.body: For each date, the team members who will work are added with their role, showing who is free and how many are still missing.

flow.title: Collect and track
flow.body: The deposit, installments and event expenses are recorded, in pesos or dollars. At month end, the summary shows what came in, what went out and what is still pending.

examples.title: What it looks like in different businesses.

items.title: Distributor or wholesaler
items.body: Orders come in over WhatsApp, inventory lives in an Excel file and nobody's quite sure what's in the warehouse. An inventory and sales system can update stock when an order is confirmed and show you what to restock before you run out.

items.title: Appointment-based business
items.body: In a clinic, a repair shop or a beauty salon, the schedule often lives in a notebook or on one person's phone. A booking system brings together the team's calendar, each client's history and the day's payments.

items.title: Event company
items.body: Dates, crew and payments spread across chats and spreadsheets. That's what EventOps solves: a calendar with site visits, setup and teardown, clients with their history, crew assigned per date and each month's results.

steps.title: A scope document

steps.title: Partial deliveries every week
steps.body: If the system is large, we split it up and start with what hurts most, like inventory or orders. Every week you see a working piece and try it with your team.

steps.title: Rollout

pricing.label: Price and timeline

afterDelivery.label: Warranty

items.question: Should I get a custom system or an off-the-shelf one?
items.answer: If an off-the-shelf system fits how you work, it may be enough. A custom system makes sense when your operation has its own steps that packaged software doesn't cover, or when you end up using three programs and a spreadsheet to fill the gaps. In the first conversation we tell you what we think fits your case.

items.question: I run everything on Excel today. What happens to that data?
items.answer: We start from there. We move your product, client or order spreadsheets into the new system, and that's planned in the proposal. If a spreadsheet still works for you, we can keep it connected.

items.question: Will my team be able to use it?
items.answer: We build it around how your team works, and they test it every week while it's being built. If you want, we add a training session so everyone can use it from day one.

items.question: Who owns the system, and what happens to my data?
items.answer: Your data is confidential and we only use it for your project. Who owns the code depends on whether it's a custom build or one of our products like EventOps. We put it in writing in the proposal before we start.

faq.title: Questions about websites, booking pages and catalogs.

items.question: Can I update prices and products myself?
items.answer: We can add a dashboard so you can edit prices, photos and products without depending on anyone. We define it in the proposal based on how often your catalog changes.

items.question: How is this different from opening a store on an e-commerce platform?
items.answer: E-commerce platforms make sense if you want checkout with a cart and automated shipping. If your customers already buy from you on WhatsApp, a catalog with WhatsApp ordering is usually simpler: they pick, message you with the order ready, and you keep selling the way you always have. We help you figure out which one fits.

items.question: Can the booking page send reminders?
items.answer: It can be included. Reminders, cancellations and rescheduling are defined in the proposal based on what your business needs.

items.question: Will the site show up on Google?
items.answer: We build it so Google can read it properly: every page with its own title, description and content, and fast on mobile. Ranking high takes time and depends on how many people search for what you offer. We do not promise rankings.

items.question: I already have an old website. Do you rebuild it or fix it?
items.answer: It depends on how it was built. We take a look, and if improving it makes more sense than starting over, we say so in the proposal.

covers.title: What we solve.
covers.body: The repeated questions that eat your day: hours, prices, stock, open slots. The bot answers what it can and escalates what it cannot. AI where it pays off, not for show.

sections.title: Where it lives.
sections.body: On WhatsApp, on your site or on the channel where people already write to you. It connects to what you already use: your calendar, catalog or spreadsheet. You do not need to replace everything to start.

audience.title: Who it is for.
audience.intro: For businesses that get a lot of questions and cannot reply on time. If your team spends hours on the same answers every day, a well-built bot takes that load off.

items.title: Shops that sell on WhatsApp
items.body: The same stock, price and shipping questions, all day long.

items.title: Appointment-based businesses
items.body: Coordinating every booking by message eats the team's hours.

items.title: Event companies
items.body: Date and quote inquiries that arrive after hours.

examples.title: What a bot can do for your business.

items.title: Shop that sells on WhatsApp
items.body: People ask all day whether something is in stock, how much it costs and whether you ship. A bot can answer with your catalog and prices, take the order and pass it to you to close payment or arrange delivery.

items.title: Appointment-based business
items.body: The bot shows open slots, books the appointment and confirms it on WhatsApp. If someone asks for something unusual, it lets you know so you can reply yourself.

items.title: Event company
items.body: Inquiries about dates and quotes arrive after hours. The bot collects the basics, like date, venue, guest count and service, and leaves the inquiry ready for you to quote.

faq.title: Questions about bots and AI agents.

items.question: Does it work with my current WhatsApp number?
items.answer: It depends on how you use that number today. We assess each case and walk you through the options before we start.

items.question: What if the bot says something wrong?
items.answer: The bot answers with the information we give it: your prices, your hours, your catalog. If it does not know something, it says so and hands the conversation to you. You test it before your customers ever see it.

items.question: What is the difference between a bot and an AI agent?
items.answer: A bot follows a set path, with menus, options and fixed answers. An AI agent understands what the customer writes in their own words and can take actions, like checking your stock or booking an appointment. We use AI where it helps resolve the request, and a simple bot when that is enough.

items.question: Can I see the conversations and reply myself?
items.answer: It can be added depending on the project, for example an inbox to review what the bot said or a direct handoff to your WhatsApp. We define it in the proposal.

items.question: Does it replace my support team?
items.answer: It takes care of the repetitive questions so your team can focus on what needs a person: a complaint, a large sale, a special case.

integraciones.metaTitle: Integrations: Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA and WhatsApp
integraciones.metaDescription: Custom integrations with Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA invoicing, AI WhatsApp bots and Google Sheets. Enter data once. Scope in writing.
integraciones.h1: Custom integrations with your current tools.
integraciones.lead: We connect Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA invoicing, WhatsApp and your spreadsheets to each other. Enter something once and it shows up where it should, without tearing down what already works.

covers.title: What we solve.
covers.body: Data that moves by hand from one place to another: an order that comes in on WhatsApp and gets typed into a spreadsheet, a sale you collect in one place and invoice in another. We connect those pieces so the data is entered once and nobody has to copy it.

items.title: Mercado Pago: payments and reconciliation
items.body: Every payment that comes in through Mercado Pago can be recorded automatically in your spreadsheet or system, linked to its order. Reconciliation stops being a line-by-line review at the end of the month, and you see right away what is paid and what is pending.

items.title: Tiendanube: stock and orders
items.body: If you sell online and in a physical shop, there should be a single stock. We sync Tiendanube inventory with your spreadsheet or system and make each new order reach whoever prepares it, without checking the dashboard.

items.title: ARCA electronic invoicing
items.body: We connect your sales to ARCA (formerly AFIP) electronic invoicing services so the invoice is issued automatically when a payment or order is confirmed. You set the rules: which receipt type, for whom and when.

items.title: AI WhatsApp bot
items.body: A WhatsApp assistant that answers common questions, takes orders or bookings and records them where they belong. When a conversation needs a person, it hands it over. We build it with your answers and your rules, not generic scripts.

items.title: Google Sheets and CRM
items.body: If your team works in Google Sheets or a CRM, we use it as the hub: orders, payments and contacts from other tools arrive there organized, and changes you make there are reflected wherever needed.

process.title: How we work and how we quote.

steps.title: A 30-minute call
steps.body: We look at how data moves today: where it comes in, where it gets copied by hand and where it gets lost. That shows which connection saves you the most work.

steps.title: A scope document
steps.body: What gets connected, what happens if something fails and what we need from you. Price and timeline in writing before we start.

steps.title: Partial deliveries every week
steps.body: We connect each tool through its official API, and every week you test a working piece with your real cases.

steps.title: Rollout
steps.body: We leave it running with your team. Every integration alerts you when something does not go as expected.

pricing.label: Price and timeline
pricing.body: We charge an implementation fee based on the complexity of the integration and, once it is running, a maintenance fee. Some tools charge for their own usage: if you already have the accounts, we use them; if not, we handle them and charge you their cost.

afterDelivery.label: Warranty
afterDelivery.body: If an integration fails because of a bug on our side, we fix it under warranty.

afterDelivery.label: Maintenance
afterDelivery.body: Covers the adjustments when an external tool changes how it connects. Without it, that adjustment is on you.

afterDelivery.label: Your data
afterDelivery.body: It's confidential and we only use it for your project.

items.question: Which tools can you connect?
items.answer: WhatsApp, Google Sheets, Mercado Pago, Tiendanube, ARCA electronic invoicing and CRMs, among other tools that offer a way to connect from outside (an API). If yours does not, we look at it in our first conversation and tell you the alternatives.

items.question: Can you connect ARCA (formerly AFIP) electronic invoicing?
items.answer: Yes. We connect your sales to ARCA so each invoice is issued without entering it by hand. In our first conversation we go over which account details are needed and help you set them up.

items.question: What happens if an integration breaks?
items.answer: We build every integration to alert you when something fails. If the bug is ours, we fix it. If an external tool you chose changes how it connects, the adjustment is on you, unless you have a maintenance plan with us.

items.question: Should I do this or build a new system?
items.answer: If what you use today works and the problem is moving data by hand, connecting is usually faster and cheaper. If your tools no longer give you what you need, a management system may make more sense. We tell you in the first conversation.

items.question: Can't I just do this myself with Zapier or Make?
items.answer: For simple connections, yes, and sometimes that is what we recommend. When there are rules specific to your business, many steps or high volume, it pays to have something custom built that you can control.

como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.title: Does your business need a website? How to know if it is worth it
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.metaTitle: Does your business need a website? How to know if it is worth it
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.metaDescription: Signs a website makes sense for your small business or shop, when it does not yet, and how to measure whether yours works. With a checklist and FAQ.
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.excerpt: Concrete signs to decide whether a website adds value to your business, when it is better to wait and how to measure whether yours is working.
como-saber-si-tu-negocio-necesita-pagina.answer: A website is worth it if people look for you on Google, if you answer the same questions all day on WhatsApp or Instagram, if you have products or services to show or if your customers need to trust you before buying. It can wait if all your customers come through referrals and you can barely keep up, if you are still testing what to sell or if you will not be able to keep the information up to date. In the meantime, a complete Google Business Profile and a WhatsApp Business catalog may be enough.
intro: Many businesses in Argentina sell well with Instagram, WhatsApp and word of mouth. So the question comes up: do you need a website, or is it just another expense? The honest answer is that it depends. A website does not sell on its own, but in some cases it saves you time, brings in inquiries you are losing today and builds trust with people who do not know you yet.
In this guide you will find concrete signs to help you decide, the cases where it is better to wait and how to measure whether the website you already have is doing its job.

sections.title: Signs a website makes sense
paragraphs: If two or more of these sound familiar, a website will probably help:
items: People look for you on Google. If someone types your business name, or something like «hardware store in Rosario», and cannot find you, those inquiries go somewhere else. A website with your information, together with a Google Business Profile, makes you show up when people search.

You answer the same questions all day. If on WhatsApp or Instagram you keep replying about prices, opening hours, delivery areas or payment methods, a website with that information gives you time back and lets customers start the conversation almost decided.
You have products or services to show. An organized catalog with photos, descriptions and prices or ranges is easier to browse than an Instagram feed or a set of PDFs you send by chat.

You need to build trust. Many customers, especially other businesses, look up your website before writing or paying. Seeing who is behind it, where you are, how you work and how to reach you lowers their doubts.
You depend on a single social network. If your account gets blocked tomorrow or the algorithm changes, you lose your storefront. A website is a place of your own that you control.
You want to take orders, bookings or inquiries without being on top of it. A form, a catalog with WhatsApp ordering or a booking system keep working while you are busy with something else.

sections.title: When you do not need one yet
paragraphs: A website is not always the priority. It can wait if:
items: All your customers come through referrals and you can barely keep up with the orders you already have.
You are still testing what to sell or to whom, and your offer changes every week.
You will not be able to keep the information up to date. A website with old prices or a phone number nobody answers does more harm than having nothing.
sections.closing: In those cases, a complete Google Business Profile and a good WhatsApp Business catalog may be enough for now. When the business grows or you find yourself answering the same things over and over, ask the question again.

sections.title: How to know if your current website works
paragraphs: If you already have a website, existing is not enough. Here are four simple ways to check whether it is doing its job:
items: Impressions and clicks in Google Search Console. It is a free Google tool that shows how many times you appeared in results (impressions), how many people clicked through (clicks) and for which searches. If you have almost no impressions, Google is not showing you. If you have impressions but few clicks, review the title and description of your pages.

Inquiries coming from the website. Ask every new customer how they found you, or use a form or a WhatsApp link that only lives on the website so you know which inquiries come from it. In the end, what matters is whether the website brings you conversations.
Speed. If the page is slow to load, many people leave before seeing it. You can measure it for free with Google PageSpeed Insights, which also tells you what is slowing it down.
How it looks on a phone. Many people will visit from their phone. Open it on yours: can you read it without zooming? Are the buttons easy to tap? Can you find the WhatsApp or phone number in seconds?
sections.closing: If the answer to any of these is «no» or «I do not know», that is where to start.

sections.title: What a website needs to be worth it
paragraphs: A useful website for a small business or shop does not need to be big. It needs to quickly answer the questions people ask you by chat today: what you do, for whom, where, how much (even if it is a range or a starting price) and how to contact you.

If it also has an up-to-date catalog, a visible WhatsApp button and loads fast on a phone, it already covers what most customers will look for. Everything else can be added later, once you know which pages people visit and which inquiries it brings.

checklist.title: Quick checklist
checklist.intro: Before deciding, go through this list:
items: Do people search for my business or what I sell on Google?
Do I answer the same questions several times a day?
Do I have products or services that are easier to understand with photos and descriptions?
Do my customers need to trust me before buying or paying in advance?
Do I depend on a single social network to be found?
Will I be able to keep the information up to date?
If I already have a website: do I know how many impressions, clicks and inquiries it brings?
checklist.closing: If you said yes to several of the first five and also to the sixth, a website is probably worth it.

items.question: Is Instagram enough instead of a website?
items.answer: For many businesses it is a good start. The difference is that the Instagram account is not yours and Google does not always show it when someone searches for what you sell. A website and social media complement each other: social media creates interest and the website organizes the information and makes you findable.

items.question: How long does a new website take to show up on Google?
items.answer: There is no fixed timeline and it depends on each site. It helps to add it to Google Search Console, submit the sitemap and have a Google Business Profile that links to the website. Search Console shows you when the first impressions start to appear.

items.question: Do I need a catalog with a shopping cart?
items.answer: Not always. If you sell few products or each sale needs a conversation, a catalog with WhatsApp ordering is usually enough. An online store with payments makes sense when the number of orders justifies it.

items.question: What if I already have a website but it brings no inquiries?
items.answer: Check the basics first: whether it shows up in Search Console, whether it loads fast, whether it looks good on a phone and whether contact details are visible. Often the website does not answer what customers are looking for, or it is hard to reach you from there.

items.question: Does a website replace WhatsApp?
items.answer: No, it complements it. The idea is that the website answers the usual questions so the WhatsApp conversation starts with an informed customer.
